newsitem.title: ITALY: Return of soft, sexy style lights up Milan fashion.
newsitem.headline: Return of soft, sexy style lights up Milan fashion.

text.p: Softness, slinkiness and colour are stealing into Italian designer womenswear after lean seasons of sexless minimalism, and the 90s woman is increasingly able to mix and match, fashion industry experts said on Sunday.

Retail trade buyers at Milan's 1997 spring/summer ready-to-wear shows said ruffles, frills and the simple dress were back with Gianni Versace, Prada and Dolce & Gabbana, while fashion house Gucci demonstrated sexy urban sleekness.
"We're moving out of an age of minimalism, with femininity and details more important than androgyny," said Barbara Atkin, fashion director at Canadian store group Holt Renfrew.
The eight days of shows were ending later on Sunday with the prime designs of top stylist Giorgio Armani. Buyers were awaiting his collection but said distinct trends had emerged.

Joan Kaner, fashion director at U.S. high-fashion retailer Neiman Marcus, saw two strong influences. "One is "put it together anyway you like' and that's very much an English attitude. It's a combination of thrift shop, a bit of the 60s and 70s and a modern edge in the way it's put together.
"The other trend is a very modern, sleek look. We saw that at Gucci and Versace," Kaner said.

Gucci's chief designer Tom Ford gave a lean show in mostly chocolate browns and black, which, after a breathtaking line-up in the previous season, left some buyers deflated. "It was good but it wasn't "Wow,'" said one buyer who declined to be named.
"People had such high expectations and that showed. I saw some very beautiful pieces but I don't think it compared with the last season," said another.
Others said Gucci had new ideas on cutting garments and Kaner added: "Gucci had a hard edge. Lots of women are not interested in ruffles or frills and they'll be happy with that."
Atkin noted jackets were disappearing from the runway although they were still on offer in the showrooms.

She said softer tailoring was emerging with blouses and knitted sweaters replacing jackets. "We're on a new millennium of dressing for women and it's going to take teaching on the selling floor to educate our women on this new sensibility."
Design duo Dolce & Gabbana also used new feminine tailoring. "They redefined the pinstripe suit so it was sexy power dressing with a real feminine edge," Atkin said.

Bridget Cosgrave, from London store Harvey Nichols, agreed. "That's Dolce's handwriting -- even if it's a pinstriped suit it's got that womanly curve to it." She noted they had nipped dresses in higher up the waist below the breast.
Miuccia Prada won praise for more femininity and greater colour. "Prada broke new ground with this femininity and by doing Chinese styles but not in an obvious way," Cosgrave said.

Prada had also spearheaded use of modern synthetic fibres. This would need customer education as "they equate synthetics with the 1960s mentality," while instead synthetics were supple as finest silk, breathable and travelled well, Atkin said.
Kaner said Versace's main collection "had a lightness, with whites, the lavenders and the beautiful jersey dresses with the frills, all done in a very sophisticated yet sexy way."
Atkin cited a shift to designerwear as status symbol, with Missoni a frontrunner to benefit after a strong line-up. "That Missoni print is recognisable and people are going to want it."
Some buyers had seen no designs which really made them sit up and said a trend of transparent clothing in the shows was unwearable and unsellable.
